title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 11
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A detergent manufacturer reformulated its product to work at lower temperatures and reports that customers who bought the new formulation used less electricity for laundry over the following year. It concludes that the reformulation reduced household electricity use.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The new formulation costs slightly more.
B. Some customers wash at high temperatures regardless of the detergent used.
C. Electricity prices rose during the year.
D. The manufacturer also sells fabric conditioner.
E. Buyers of the new formulation were recruited from a mailing list of customers who had already been washing at low temperatures.
questions.explanation: The comparison group was pre-selected for the behaviour being measured, so their low usage need owe nothing to the product. D would affect all households and so cannot explain a difference between them.

questions.prompt: A taxi application raises fares when demand is high, arguing that this brings more drivers onto the road and so reduces waiting times for passengers.
questions.question: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Passengers are willing to pay the higher fares.
B. The application has no competitors in the market.
C. Fares return to normal levels promptly.
D. Enough drivers respond to higher fares by working at times they otherwise would not.
E. Drivers are self-employed.
questions.explanation: The mechanism requires supply to be responsive; if drivers cannot or will not shift their hours, the price rise rations demand without adding cars. A concerns whether passengers accept the outcome, not whether waiting times fall.

questions.prompt: A school district reports that pupils who take three science subjects achieve higher university admission rates than those who take one, and proposes requiring all pupils to take three sciences.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. Pupils currently choose three sciences when they are already strong in the subject and intend to apply for competitive courses.
B. Science laboratories are expensive to equip.
C. Some universities do not require science subjects.
D. Pupils taking three sciences study fewer other subjects.
E. Admission rates vary by year.
questions.explanation: The association reflects who chooses the option, so compelling everyone need not raise admission rates and may lower them for pupils whose strengths lie elsewhere.

questions.prompt: An upland estate reduced the number of sheep grazing a hillside and, three years later, the variety of plant species on the hill had increased. The estate manager concludes that reduced grazing caused the increase.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The hillside is popular with walkers.
B. Sheep prefer certain plant species to others.
C. On an adjacent hillside with the same soil, aspect and weather, where stocking was unchanged, plant variety did not increase over the same period.
D. The estate also repaired its boundary walls.
E. Rainfall was slightly above average in two of the three years.
questions.explanation: A matched control removes weather and soil as explanations, which E would otherwise supply. C makes the mechanism plausible but is far weaker evidence.

questions.prompt: Every branch of the Aldercroft bank that offers business banking is open on Saturday mornings. No branch open on Saturday mornings has been scheduled for closure. Some branches have been scheduled for closure.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Business banking is profitable.
B. Some branches do not offer business banking.
C. Every branch open on Saturday offers business banking.
D. Most branches are open on Saturday mornings.
E. Branches scheduled for closure have few customers.
questions.explanation: Branches scheduled for closure exist; such a branch is not open on Saturdays, and business banking implies Saturday opening, so those branches do not offer it. C reverses the conditional.

questions.prompt: A warehouse operator introduced a safety campaign and reports that recorded accidents fell by 40 per cent in the following year. A safety inspector is sceptical that conditions have genuinely improved.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the inspector's scepticism?
options: A. Whether the campaign included posters as well as training
B. How much the campaign cost
C. Whether staff enjoyed the training sessions
D. How many staff the warehouse employs
E. Whether the reporting procedure or the threshold for recording an accident changed at the same time
questions.explanation: A change in what counts as a recordable accident would produce the fall without any change in conditions, which is precisely the inspector's concern.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain introduced cups that can be recycled and announced that its packaging waste is now recyclable. Environmental campaigners note that the cups are accepted by only a small number of specialist facilities.
questions.question: The campaigners' point weakens the chain's announcement by
options: A. showing that the cups are made of unsuitable material
B. distinguishing what is technically recyclable from what is actually recycled in practice
C. questioning the chain's environmental commitment generally
D. arguing that reusable cups are preferable
E. demonstrating that customers do not sort their waste
questions.explanation: The gap between capability and infrastructure is the specific defect; the claim may be literally true and practically empty.

questions.prompt: A marathon reduced its entry fee and received twice as many applications. The organisers conclude that the fee had been deterring runners.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The race is held on a Sunday.
B. Some applicants withdraw before race day.
C. Entry fees for comparable races are higher.
D. The reduction was announced alongside a change of route that removed the event's steepest section, which runners had complained about for years.
E. The organisers advertised in running magazines, as in previous years.
questions.explanation: A simultaneous change addressing a known complaint offers an alternative explanation for the surge. E explicitly holds advertising constant and so removes rather than adds a rival cause.

questions.prompt: A greenhouse grower found that tomato plants given supplementary lighting yielded more fruit than unlit plants, and concludes that installing lighting throughout the greenhouse will raise total yield proportionately.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes the cost of electricity will not rise
B. ignores consumer preferences for tomato varieties
C. overlooks that the lit plants may have benefited from being in the warmest part of the greenhouse, where the lights were installed
D. does not specify the duration of lighting
E. relies on a single growing season
questions.explanation: Position confounds the comparison: heat and light arrived together, so the yield difference cannot be attributed to lighting alone.

questions.prompt: A radio station found that listeners recall advertisements broadcast in the morning better than those broadcast at night, and advises advertisers that morning slots are more effective.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advice?
options: A. Night-time listeners are far fewer but buy the advertised products at a much higher rate, so cost per sale is lower at night.
B. Morning slots cost more than night slots.
C. Recall is measured by telephone survey.
D. Some listeners hear the same advertisement at both times.
E. The station's audience is largest at midday.
questions.explanation: Recall is an intermediate measure; if the commercial outcome runs the other way, advice based on recall is wrong. A bears on price without addressing effectiveness.

questions.prompt: A company introduced a wellness programme and reports that participating employees took fewer sick days than non-participants, presenting this as evidence that the programme improves health.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the presentation?
options: A. The programme includes exercise classes and dietary advice.
B. The programme is voluntary, and employees with chronic conditions are least able to attend its sessions.
C. Participation was higher in the first year than the second.
D. Sick days are recorded by managers.
E. Some participants attend only occasionally.
questions.explanation: The selection runs directly against the conclusion: those most likely to be ill are least likely to participate, so the gap would appear with no effect at all.

questions.passageText:
Online ratings are widely treated as an aggregate of experience, and they are, but the aggregation is not of a representative sample. Three selection effects operate at once, and they do not cancel.

The first is who writes. Reviewing is unpaid and costs time, so it attracts the unusually satisfied and the unusually aggrieved, producing the characteristic distribution in which extreme scores outnumber middling ones. The second is who buys. A product is bought disproportionately by the customers most likely to want it, so its reviewers are drawn from a favourably disposed group, and a niche product may score higher than a superior general one simply because its buyers selected themselves better. The third is who continues. Ratings on subscription services are dominated by current users; those who found the service unsuitable have left and are silent.

These effects can be partially corrected. Verified-purchase filters help with fraud but not with self-selection. Weighting by reviewer history helps a little. What helps most is comparison of like with like — the same category, the same buyer population — rather than treatment of the score as an absolute measure.

The practical consequence for sellers is uncomfortable. A firm can raise its rating by narrowing its market, since a product sold only to those who will love it collects better reviews than one sold widely. The score rewards a strategy that a firm seeking growth cannot pursue, which is one reason ratings correlate less well with quality than their prominence suggests.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the distribution of online ratings tends to show more extreme than middling scores because
options: A. most products are either very good or very bad
B. platforms remove moderate reviews
C. buyers cannot compare products directly
D. sellers solicit reviews from friends
E. reviewing costs time, so it attracts the unusually satisfied and the unusually aggrieved
questions.explanation: The first selection effect. C and E describe manipulation, which the passage treats separately under fraud.

options: A. it is usually more expensive
B. it receives fewer reviews overall
C. its reviewers are more experienced
D. its buyers have selected themselves more accurately into the group likely to want it

questions.passageText:
Injecting reflective particles into the stratosphere would cool the Earth's surface. The physics is not seriously disputed: large volcanic eruptions have done it, and the resulting temperature drops have been measured. The difficulty with solar geoengineering lies almost entirely elsewhere.

The first problem is that it addresses temperature, not carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification would continue unaffected, since it depends on how much carbon dioxide dissolves rather than on how warm the surface is. A programme that cooled the planet while emissions continued would leave that damage untouched, and would create a growing gap between the actual concentration and the temperature it would otherwise produce.

That gap creates the second problem. If injection stopped — through cost, conflict or a change of government — temperatures would rise rapidly toward the level the accumulated carbon dioxide implies, and the rate of that rise would be far more damaging than the same warming spread over decades. A programme once begun would have to be continued for as long as the excess concentration persists, which is a commitment no institution has demonstrated it can honour.

The third problem is distributional. Any intervention would alter regional rainfall unevenly, benefiting some regions and harming others, and no procedure exists for deciding who chooses the setting. The research question and the governance question are therefore not separable, and the strongest argument for studying the technique is not that it should be used, but that a state facing catastrophe may attempt it regardless, and ignorance is a poor preparation for that.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that solar geoengineering would not address
options: A. ocean acidification
B. surface temperature
C. regional rainfall
D. the cost of emissions reduction
E. volcanic cooling
questions.explanation: Acidification depends on dissolved carbon dioxide rather than surface warmth, so cooling leaves it untouched.

questions.passageTitle: What GDP Was Built to Do
questions.passageText:
National income accounting was developed in the 1930s and 1940s to answer specific questions: how much slack existed in a depressed economy, and how much a wartime economy could produce. It answered them well, and the criticisms now made of gross domestic product are largely complaints that it does not answer other questions it was never designed for.

The familiar objections are correct as far as they go. GDP counts activity rather than welfare; it treats expenditure on repairing damage as positive; it omits household work and volunteering; it says nothing about distribution, so a rise consistent with falling incomes for most people is arithmetically unremarkable; and it ignores depletion of natural assets, treating the liquidation of a stock as current income.

The proposed remedies divide into two kinds. One would adjust the aggregate, subtracting environmental damage or adding household production to produce a single better number. The other would leave GDP alone and publish a dashboard of indicators alongside it. Each has a characteristic failing: adjusted aggregates bury contestable value judgements inside a figure that looks technical, while dashboards are easy to ignore precisely because they offer no single number for a headline.

There is a reason the aggregate persists that its critics rarely address. Policy requires comparison across countries and over time, and GDP is measured with a consistency that no proposed replacement has yet matched. The reasonable position treats it as an indicator of one thing, measured well, and treats the demand that it also measure welfare as the source of most of the confusion.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that most criticisms of GDP are
options: A. factually mistaken
B. motivated by political disagreement
C. complaints that it does not answer questions it was not designed for
D. based on measurement errors in the underlying data
E. confined to environmental concerns
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph, and the second paragraph then grants that the objections are correct as far as they go.

questions.passageText:
Deciding who made a work is among the older problems in the humanities, and the statistical methods now applied to it have a mixed record that repays examination.

Stylometry rests on the observation that writers differ measurably in features they do not consciously control: the frequency of common function words, sentence-length distributions, patterns of collocation. These are more useful than vocabulary or subject matter precisely because they are unconscious and therefore hard to imitate deliberately.

The method has produced genuinely convincing results where conditions are favourable — a closed set of candidate authors, substantial samples from each, and texts of the same genre and period. Where conditions are unfavourable, it produces confident answers that are worth very little. Genre affects function-word frequencies as strongly as authorship does, so comparing a play with a pamphlet may measure the difference between forms rather than between people. Collaborative and edited texts have no single author to detect. And an open candidate set permits the method to name the closest of the authors considered while the true author was never in the comparison.

The soundest current practice treats attribution as a question of relative probability rather than identification, states the candidate set explicitly, and requires that a result survive several independent methods. Where the humanities have been badly served is not by the statistics but by their reporting: a finding that one author is somewhat more probable than another, given a particular set of assumptions, becomes in summary a discovery that a text was written by a named person.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that function words are useful in attribution because they are
options: A. specific to particular genres
B. unconscious and therefore hard to imitate deliberately
C. rare enough to be counted accurately
D. unaffected by editing
E. consistent across languages
questions.explanation: That is the stated reason they are preferred to vocabulary or subject matter. A is in fact one of the method's problems.

Deciding who made a work is among the older problems in the humanities, and the statistical methods now applied to it have a mixed record that repays examination.

Stylometry rests on the observation that writers differ measurably in features they do not consciously control: the frequency of common function words, sentence-length distributions, patterns of collocation. These are more useful than vocabulary or subject matter precisely because they are unconscious and therefore hard to imitate deliberately.

The method has produced genuinely convincing results where conditions are favourable — a closed set of candidate authors, substantial samples from each, and texts of the same genre and period. Where conditions are unfavourable, it produces confident answers that are worth very little. Genre affects function-word frequencies as strongly as authorship does, so comparing a play with a pamphlet may measure the difference between forms rather than between people. Collaborative and edited texts have no single author to detect. And an open candidate set permits the method to name the closest of the authors considered while the true author was never in the comparison.

The soundest current practice treats attribution as a question of relative probability rather than identification, states the candidate set explicitly, and requires that a result survive several independent methods. Where the humanities have been badly served is not by the statistics but by their reporting: a finding that one author is somewhat more probable than another, given a particular set of assumptions, becomes in summary a discovery that a text was written by a named person.
